chapter_title: Before We Go, Part 2: Traveling Well and the Learning for All Thread
learning_objective: The learner will classify twelve writing systems as logographic, syllabary, abjad, or alphabet from what one basic sign stands for and how many signs the script uses, with at least 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** sort-the-scripts
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Understand
**Bloom Verb:** classify
**Learning Objective:** The learner will classify twelve writing systems as logographic, syllabary, abjad, or alphabet from what one basic sign stands for and how many signs the script uses, with at least 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt. **Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/computer-science/tree/main/docs/sims/symbol-character-quiz
**Prerequisites:** writing system, logographic script, syllabary, abjad, alphabet, the sign-count rule of thumb (all defined in the section "Writing Systems" above); Linear A and Linear B (introduced in Part 1). **Evidence of Mastery:** For each script card, the learner assigns it to one of four bins. An assignment is correct when it matches the Correct kind column in Content. Mastery is 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt. Reading a card is exploration; the committed assignment is the evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) Egyptian hieroglyphs are an alphabet because some signs stand for single sounds. (2) Hebrew and Arabic are alphabets in the same sense as Greek. (3) A script nobody can read cannot be classified. (4) Alphabets are always older than syllabaries. **Instructional Rationale:** Classifying new cases by a defining rule is Understand-level work. Each card gives the learner the two pieces of evidence the chapter teaches (what one sign stands for, and how many signs there are), so the learner must apply the definitions rather than recognize names; three cards target the three most common confusions. **Content:** Four bins: Logographic (most signs stand for words or parts of words); Syllabary (each sign stands for a syllable); Abjad (each sign stands for a consonant; most vowels are left to the reader); Alphabet (signs for vowels and consonants alike). Cards, presented in shuffled order: | # | Card text shown to the learner | Correct kind | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Egyptian hieroglyphs: several hundred signs; most stand for words or ideas, and some stand for one or two consonant sounds. | Logographic | A few sound-signs do not make an alphabet; with hundreds of signs mostly standing for words, it is logographic. | | 2 | Chinese characters: a newspaper reader needs about 3,000 to 4,000; each usually stands for a syllable that is also a word or part of a word. | Logographic | Thousands of signs, each tied to a meaning, mark a logographic script. | | 3 | Linear A (Minoan Crete, undeciphered): about 90 signs, many shared with Linear B. | Syllabary | We cannot read it, but about 90 signs fits a syllabary, and its signs match Linear B's syllable signs. | | 4 | Linear B (Mycenaean Greek): about 90 sound-signs, each a consonant plus a vowel, plus word-signs for goods. | Syllabary | Each sound-sign stands for a whole syllable: Knossos is spelled *ko-no-so*. | | 5 | Japanese hiragana: 46 basic signs, each a vowel or a consonant plus a vowel. | Syllabary | Each sign is a whole syllable: か is *ka* and み is *mi*. | | 6 | Cherokee: 85 signs, created by Sequoyah around 1821, each a syllable. | Syllabary | Each of the 85 signs stands for a syllable. | | 7 | Phoenician: 22 letters, all for consonants. | Abjad | Only consonants are written; the reader supplies the vowels. | | 8 | Hebrew: 22 letters for consonants; vowel marks are optional and usually left out. | Abjad | Without the optional marks, vowels are left to the reader. | | 9 | Arabic, as used for Ottoman Turkish until 1928: 28 letters, with most short vowels not written. | Abjad | Most vowels are not written, which made it a poor fit for Turkish, a language with eight vowels. | | 10 | Greek: 24 letters, with separate letters for vowels, including alpha and omicron. | Alphabet | Vowels and consonants each have their own letters. | | 11 | Latin, as used for English: 26 letters for vowels and consonants. | Alphabet | It came from Greek, through the Etruscans, and kept the vowel letters. | | 12 | Modern Turkish: 29 Latin letters, including ı, ö, ü, ç, ş, and ğ. | Alphabet | It writes all eight Turkish vowels with their own letters. | **Provenance:** Sign counts for Linear A and Linear B and the Linear B description come from Part 1 and the section "Writing Systems" in this chapter. Counts for hieroglyphs, Chinese characters, hiragana, Cherokee, Phoenician, Hebrew, Arabic, Greek, Latin, and Turkish are standard figures from each script's Wikipedia article; the generator must check each count against that article and keep the card text only if it still matches. The eight vowels of Turkish are from the Wikipedia article "Turkish alphabet." **Rules:** Each card has exactly one correct kind. Classification is by what most basic signs stand for, not by the presence of a few signs of another kind. An undeciphered script is classified by its sign count and its relation to known scripts. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner sees the first card and the four bins with their definitions. 2. The learner assigns the card to a bin. The card's correctness and the Why text appear, and the card moves to its correct bin. 3. The learner continues until all twelve cards are placed. 4. At the end, the learner sees the four bins filled, with each script's sign count shown, sorted from most signs to fewest. 5. The learner should notice that sign counts fall into the bands of the chapter's rule of thumb: hundreds or more for logographic, about 40 to 100 for syllabaries, under 40 for abjads and alphabets. **Feedback:** Twelve cards, shuffled once at the start, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: ." plus the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite: this is a(n) ." plus the Why text. The correct bin is shown after every answer. A running score "Correct: n of 12" is shown. At the end: "10 or more: you can tell scripts apart" or "Fewer than 10: reread the four kinds of writing system and try again." A Restart button reshuffles and clears the score. **Starting State:** Four empty bins with their definitions, one card face up, and the prompt "What does one sign stand for in this script?" **Chapter Anchors:** Four kinds of writing system. Linear B has about 90 signs. Phoenician, Hebrew and Arabic have 22 to 28 letters. Under about 40 signs suggests an alphabet or abjad, about 40 to 100 a syllabary, hundreds or more a logographic script. Writing was invented independently at least four times.
